newsitem.title: USA: Brazil insect helps protect African cassava crops.
newsitem.headline: Brazil insect helps protect African cassava crops.

text.p: A tiny Brazilian insect can protect African cassava crops from a pest that destroys the starchy root vegetable eaten by millions of people, a team of international scientists said on Tuesday.

The use of a natural enemy imported from South America to fight the cassava green mites can boost cassava production by as much as 30 percent, officials at the International Center for Tropical Agriculture said.

An experiment with introducing the aripo, a tiny beneficial mite the size of a period, showed cassava production increased by about US$60 million in Benin, Cameroon, Ghana and Nigeria, according to scientists.

"The benefits of this are tremendous," said Lincoln Smith, an entomologist with the Colombian-based Center for Tropical Agriculture. "Cassava is the kind of thing that every African farmer grows in his backyard to provide food throughout the year."

Cassava, also known as yuca and manioc, is an important food for some 200 million people living in Africa's poorest countries because it flourishes during droughts and other harsh conditions. It is also widely eaten in Latin America.
It grows as a shrub and produces underground tubers similar to potatoes. The harvested tubers can be boiled, fried or ground into flour.

Most plants have natural defenses such as beneficial insects, but when cassava from Latin America was introduced to Africa several centuries ago, it left behind its natural protectors against the predator green mites, Smith said.
In the 1970s, the Latin American green mite arrived in Uganda and rapidly spread across Africa.

"In the absence of natural controls, the mite swept through Africa's cassava belt, destroying from one-third to more than half of the crop depending on weather, soil and other conditions," said Steve Yaninek, a researcher in Benin.

Smith, working with scientists from the Nigeria-based International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Brazil's Agricultural Research Enterprise, used computer models to determine the best South American mite to guard cassava from pests.
"We travelled South America to find out what kinds of predators existed, then we evaluated them to make sure they wouldn't cause other problems if transplanted to Africa," he said.
After comparing climate data, the scientists settled on the aripo, which kills the pests that try to feed on the tips of the cassava plant.

The aripo protects cassava against the green mites but other technicques will need to be developed to fight the African mosaic virus, which is transmitted by the white fly and attacks the leaves of the plants, Smith said.
